# Cloning a project — product notes

_Written while scoping the "duplicate project" action (2026-01). Kept for history; see `docs/adr/0012-cloning-a-project.md` for the current rules._

## Why

Release trains and onboarding checklists are the same project over and over. People want
"duplicate" on the project page.

## What we'd like

- A "Duplicate project…" entry asking for a name; the slug and key are derived from it.
- Everything comes along: the issues with their status and assignee, so the board of the copy
  looks exactly like the board of the original; archived issues too, so the history is complete.
- Issue numbers are kept, so cross-references in descriptions ("see PLAT-12") still make sense
  in the copy.
- Comments are not copied (they are conversations, not work).
- The copy is announced like any new project, and each copied issue like any new issue, so the
  people assigned to them hear about it.

## Open questions

- Plan limits: a copy of a big project could blow the per-project issue limit. Leaning towards
  copying as many as fit and telling the user.

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type parameter to select which agent type to use. If omitted, the general-purpose agent is used.

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your one lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

# ADR 0012 — Cloning a project

- Status: accepted
- Date: 2026-03-25
- Supersedes: `docs/product/project-clone-notes.md` where the two disagree.

## Context

Teams run the same shape of project repeatedly (a release train, an onboarding checklist) and
want to start the next one from the last. The product wants a "clone project" action that
creates a new project from an existing one, optionally with its issues. Issues are numbered per
project, counted per project against the plan, indexed for search and metered for usage, so a
clone is a batch of creations and has to behave like one. This record fixes what is copied,
what is reset, and how the batch is gated.

## Decision

1. **The clone is a new project of the same workspace**, with the name, slug and key the caller
   chose. Its description, visibility, colour and lead are copied from the source. It starts
   `active`, with no start or target date, and it is not archived. The slug is treated exactly
   like a created project's slug (made unique by suffix when taken). The key is the caller's
   responsibility.

2. **Gates, like a creation.** Cloning needs the permission to read the source project and the
   permission to create a project, both checked against the acting member. The source must be a
   live project of the workspace. The plan's project quota applies as it does to creating a
   project.

3. **A clone is a fresh start.** When issues are included, every **live** (not archived) issue of
   the source is copied; archived issues are not. Each copy keeps the source issue's title,
   description, priority, estimate, due date and labels. Everything that records progress is
   reset: the copy starts in the workspace's default issue status, unassigned, with no start or
   completion time, authored by the person cloning. Comments and attachments are not copied,
   and whatever an issue is linked to is not copied either.

4. **Numbering.** The copies are numbered from 1 in the order of the source issues' numbers, so
   the clone reads in the same order as the source; issues created in the clone afterwards
   continue after them.

5. **All or nothing.** The clone is checked before anything is written: the plan's per-project
   issue quota applies to the whole batch of copies (as many issues as would be copied, counted
   the way a single creation counts them). If the batch does not fit, the clone is refused and
   nothing is created — no project, no issues.

6. **Announcing.** A clone publishes exactly one domain event, `project.cloned`, and records one
   audit entry under the new project. It does not publish `project.created` or one
   `issue.created` per copy. The things those announcements would have driven still happen:
   the clone and its issues are searchable at once, and the workspace's project and issue
   meters reflect the clone at once.

## Consequences

- Copying must walk every live issue of the source, however many there are; a page is not a
  project.
- Whatever the copier borrows, a copy never keeps the source row's status, assignee or number
  (rules 3 and 4).

   213	export async function duplicateProject(

   217	  slug: string,
   218	  key: string,
   219	): Promise<Project> {

   221	    .select()

   223	    .where(and(orgPredicate(projects.orgId, orgId), eq(projects.id, projectId)))
   224	    .get();
   225	  if (!source) throw new Error(`Project ${projectId} not found`);
   226	
   227	  const stamp = toIsoTimestamp(new Date());
   228	  const row = getDb()
   229	    .insert(projects)
   230	    .values({
   231	      ...source,
   232	      id: newId(),
   233	      name,
   234	      slug,
   235	      key,
   236	      createdAt: stamp,
   237	      updatedAt: stamp,
   238	    })
   239	    .returning()
   240	    .get();
   241	
   242	  return toProject(row);
   243	}

   245	/** Includes archived slugs — a restored project must not collide. */
   246	export async function listTakenProjectSlugs(
   247	  orgId: OrgId,
   248	): Promise<readonly string[]> {
   249	  const rows = getDb()
   250	    .select({ slug: projects.slug })
   251	    .from(projects)
   252	    .where(orgPredicate(projects.orgId, orgId))
   253	    .all();
   254	  return rows.map((row) => row.slug);
   255	}
   256	
   257	/** Open/closed/overdue counters plus the last write, for the project card. */
   258	export async function getProjectStats(
   259	  orgId: OrgId,
   260	  projectId: ProjectId,
   261	): Promise<ProjectStats> {
   262	  const db = getDb();
   263	  const scope = and(
   264	    orgPredicate(issues.orgId, orgId),
   265	    eq(issues.projectId, projectId),
   266	    ...compact(livePredicate(issues.archivedAt, {})),
   267	  );
   268	
   269	  const closed = db
   270	    .select({ value: count() })
   271	    .from(issues)
   272	    .where(and(scope, inArray(issues.status, [...CLOSED_ISSUE_STATUSES])))
   273	    .get();
   274	
   275	  const all = db.select({ value: count() }).from(issues).where(scope).get();
   276	
   277	  const overdue = db
   278	    .select({ value: count() })
   279	    .from(issues)
   280	    .where(
   281	      and(
   282	        scope,
   283	        isNotNull(issues.dueAt),
   284	        lt(issues.dueAt, toIsoTimestamp(new Date())),
   285	      ),
   286	    )
   287	    .get();
   288	
   289	  const lastActivity = db
   290	    .select({ value: sql<string | null>`max(${issues.updatedAt})` })
   291	    .from(issues)
   292	    .where(scope)
   293	    .get();
   294	
   295	  const closedCount = closed?.value ?? 0;
   296	
   297	  return {
   298	    projectId,
   299	    openIssues: (all?.value ?? 0) - closedCount,
   300	    closedIssues: closedCount,
   301	    overdueIssues: overdue?.value ?? 0,
   302	    lastActivityAt:
   303	      lastActivity?.value == null ? null : toIsoTimestamp(lastActivity.value),
   304	  };
   305	}

   258	export async function getProjectStats(
   259	  orgId: OrgId,
   260	  projectId: ProjectId,
   261	): Promise<ProjectStats> {
   262	  const db = getDb();
   263	  const scope = and(
   264	    orgPredicate(issues.orgId, orgId),
   265	    eq(issues.projectId, projectId),
   266	    ...compact(livePredicate(issues.archivedAt, {})),
   267	  );
   268	
   269	  const closed = db
   270	    .select({ value: count() })
   271	    .from(issues)
   272	    .where(and(scope, inArray(issues.status, [...CLOSED_ISSUE_STATUSES])))
   273	    .get();
   274	
   275	  const all = db.select({ value: count() }).from(issues).where(scope).get();
   276	
   277	  const overdue = db
   278	    .select({ value: count() })
   279	    .from(issues)
   280	    .where(
   281	      and(
   282	        scope,
   283	        isNotNull(issues.dueAt),
   284	        lt(issues.dueAt, toIsoTimestamp(new Date())),
   285	      ),
   286	    )
   287	    .get();
   288	
   289	  const lastActivity = db
   290	    .select({ value: sql<string | null>`max(${issues.updatedAt})` })
   291	    .from(issues)
   292	    .where(scope)
   293	    .get();

   295	  const closedCount = closed?.value ?? 0;

   299	    openIssues: (all?.value ?? 0) - closedCount,
   300	    closedIssues: closedCount,
   301	    overdueIssues: overdue?.value ?? 0,
   302	    lastActivityAt:
   303	      lastActivity?.value == null ? null : toIsoTimestamp(lastActivity.value),
   304	  };

     6	 * so a page boundary is stable even when two rows share a `created_at`.
     7	 */
     8	import { sql } from "drizzle-orm";
     9	import { decodeCursor, encodeCursor } from "./base-repository";
    10	import { makePage } from "@/types/common";
    11	import type { Page } from "@/types/common";
    12	import type { SQL } from "drizzle-orm";
    13	import type { SQLiteColumn } from "drizzle-orm/sqlite-core";
    14	
    15	export interface KeysetSort {
    16	  readonly sortColumn: SQLiteColumn;
    17	  readonly idColumn: SQLiteColumn;
    18	}
    19	
    20	/**
    21	 * Predicate that resumes a descending listing after `cursor`. Returns
    22	 * `undefined` for a first page or an unparseable cursor — a bad cursor
    23	 * degrades to "start from the top", never to an error page.
    24	 */
    25	export function keysetPredicate(
    26	  sort: KeysetSort,
    27	  cursor: string | null | undefined,
    28	): SQL | undefined {
    29	  if (!cursor) return undefined;
    30	  const decoded = decodeCursor(cursor);
    31	  if (!decoded) return undefined;
    32	
    33	  return sql`(${sort.sortColumn}, ${sort.idColumn}) < (${decoded.sortValue}, ${decoded.id})`;
    34	}
    35	
    36	/** SQLite tolerates a `LIMIT` of `n + 1`; that extra row is the has-more probe. */
    37	export function probeLimit(limit: number): number {
    38	  return Math.max(1, Math.min(limit, 100)) + 1;
    39	}
    40	
    41	/**
    42	 * Turns an over-fetched row array into a `Page`, dropping the probe row and
    43	 * deriving the next cursor from the last row that survived.
    44	 */
    45	export function toPage<TRow, TOut>(
    46	  rows: readonly TRow[],
    47	  limit: number,
    48	  total: number,
    49	  map: (row: TRow) => TOut,
    50	  cursorOf: (row: TRow) => { id: string; sortValue: string },
    51	): Page<TOut> {
    52	  const capped = Math.max(1, Math.min(limit, 100));
    53	  const hasMore = rows.length > capped;
    54	  const visible = hasMore ? rows.slice(0, capped) : rows;
    55	  const last = visible.at(-1);
    56	
    57	  const nextCursor =
    58	    hasMore && last
    59	      ? encodeCursor(cursorOf(last).id, cursorOf(last).sortValue)
    60	      : null;
    61	
    62	  return makePage(visible.map(map), nextCursor, total);
    63	}
    64	
    65	/** Drops the `undefined` slots so `and(...)` never sees a hole. */
    66	export function compact(
    67	  ...predicates: readonly (SQL | undefined)[]
    68	): readonly SQL[] {
    69	  return predicates.filter((value): value is SQL => value !== undefined);
    70	}

content.text:
The clone backend is in place. The full suite passes (74 files, 629 tests), `tsc --noEmit` is clean, and ESLint is clean on the changed files.

Choices the spec left open:
- **Copy status:** copies start in the workspace's `org.settings.defaultIssueStatus`, re-validated with a fallback to `backlog`, the same way the new-issue form does it.
- **Atomicity:** all quota checks run before any write. The project row and its copies are written in one SQLite transaction.
- **Beyond the four listed exports:** I added two repository functions, `listAllLiveIssues` (pages through every live issue) and `insertClonedProject` (the transactional write). If you want them module-private, that's a small change.
- **Webhooks:** `project.cloned` is not added to the webhook event list, since the spec doesn't mention webhooks.

I also added `tests/services/project-clone.test.ts` and one schema test in `tests/schemas/project.schema.test.ts`. No existing visible test encoded the changed behaviour, so none needed updating.
